 AIKEN — It's not news that Aiken is a Republican stronghold and has been for decades.
 “We are a red city in a red county in a red state," an Aiken County Republican Party official once said.
 Dr. Annie Andrews, though, is undeterred. As the Democratic candidate running for U.S. Senate, she ventured into GOP territory Oct. 23 to hold a town hall that was billed as "Republicans and Independents for Annie." It was not a fundraising event.
 At the Woodside home of Scott and Mary Ruth Singer, Andrews made brief remarks and answered questions from an audience of a few dozen people who gathered in the living room.
 Andrews touched on familiar issues including healthcare, the economy and building a brighter future for South Carolinians.
 “This campaign is not just for Democrats in South Carolina,” Andrews said. “It’s for independents who feel ready for change. For Republicans like my own dad who don’t recognize the current version of their political party.
 “This campaign is for everyone. It’s for people who are more concerned about their bills, about closing rural hospitals, about integrity in Washington, D.C., than they are about their own political party.”
 Andrews is running for the U.S. Senate seat vacated by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham after his death in July.
 Her opponent is Darline Graham, the sister of the late senator who was appointed to the seat by S.C. Gov. Henry McMaster. She later won a runoff in the Republican primary to earn her spot on the Nov. 3 ballot.
 Some of the attendees who asked questions said they typically voted Republican, but had either changed their mind or were considering a vote for Andrews.
 “I’m from the South, so I never voted Democrat. I’ve always voted Republican,” said Greg Burkes, an Aiken resident. “I consider myself a Reagan Republican. This isn’t a Reagan Republican Party.
 “What I see is not what I believe in. I’m a fiscal conservative, but I’m also a social liberal. I don’t care how you live your life as long as you don’t break the law.”
 Scott Singer served on Aiken County Council as a Republican. With his dissatisfaction in the current Republican administration, he felt compelled to host the event for Andrews.
 “I don’t agree with Annie Andrews on every issue,” he said. “But she has one thing really going for her that Darline Nordone has shown she does not: strength of character to perform her duty as a check and balance against the president of the United States.”
 Singer cited President Trump’s recent executive order to suspend sanctions against Russia that were meant to help end Russian President Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine. The bill was named for Lindsey Graham, who supported it before his death.
 “She (Darline Graham) could have stood up at that point and said it was wrong. What happened? Mum’s the word, she was quiet,” Singer said. “I want someone who’s going to go up there and do the things they are supposed to and represent the people of South Carolina. Not a constituency of one.”
 Trump campaigned in the Upstate recently for Graham, but she said she didn't have a chance to speak to him about the Russia issue.
 “That’s a private conversation,” Graham told The Post and Courier.
 One woman who didn’t want to use her name said she came to the event out of coincidence. She is a neighbor of the Singers, but admitted she typically votes Republican.
 “Now I’m questioning that,” she said of the Senate race.
 She questioned Andrews about how she would approach military issues, specifically benefits for family members. She stuck around after the event so she could personally talk to Andrews.
 Andrews spent about an hour at the event and answered a handful of questions, including ones on Savannah River Site, schools and gun violence, insurance and cost of living increases for retirees.
 “I got into this as a mom and a pediatrician, not as a member of any political party,” Andrews said after the event. “Of course, I’m running as a Democrat, but as I said this campaign is for everybody. Because everyone is frustrated. 
 “We’ve got to do something different, try something different. That’s what I’m offering, and I’m looking forward to getting support from every corner of the state.” 
 Aiken resident Jim Kabel said he appreciated the chance to hear from the candidate in person.
 "This event was useful to get that up close and personal understanding of who she really is," he said. "I would characterize myself as a Democrat but one of the most moderate ones. I really do like to listen to all the issues. I like to hear about all sides of the media that’s out there."
